items.title: Malacia has 'no regrets' over Man Utd - despite having to train with kids
items.content: <article>Tyrell Malacia opens up on his time at Manchester United after moving to FC Cincinnati to restart his career in Major League Soccer.</article>
items.lbText:
Tyrell Malacia has no regrets about joining Manchester United even if he had to train with the club's youth players after former manager Ruben Amorim exiled him to his 'bomb squad'.

Dutch left-back Malacia is rebuilding his career in Major League Soccer with FC Cincinnati after his United contract expired in the summer.

The 27-year-old is eager to point out he is fully fit and has been since November 2024, when he returned after a year and a half out following two major knee operations.

Malacia's appearance for FC Cincinnati in their 2-1 victory over DC United on 21 October was the first time he had started four successive games since September 2022, at the beginning of his first season with the Old Trafford outfit following a £13m move from Feyenoord.

That debut campaign under fellow countryman Erik ten Hag was Malacia's high point as a United player, playing 39 times across all competitions.

As it turned out, he would only feature on another 11 occasions in the next three seasons.

"I wouldn't regret anything, not one bit," he said in an exclusive interview with BBC Sport. "Even if I could do it over, I would do the same thing because otherwise I wouldn't be the man I am now."

That is not to say Malacia is at ease with how it worked out at Old Trafford, even if there is at least an understanding of where Michael Carrick was coming from when the door was closed on the defender leaving in January to ensure United had enough cover if Luke Shaw got injured - which, ironically given how the current campaign is turning out, he never did.

The problem started when Malacia returned for pre-season training in the summer of 2023.

As he recounted in an interview with The Athletic in November 2024, Malacia had ended the 2022-23 campaign feeling discomfort in his left knee. He hoped it would go away in the summer, but it did not. He returned to the Netherlands for surgery, but the healing process did not go as planned and he needed a second operation.

Malacia does not want to go into details but, when he eventually made his comeback, for the Under-21 side in an EFL Trophy defeat at Huddersfield, he expected it to be the start of a road back to the first team, which by now was under the control of Amorim after Ten Hag's dismissal.

"I had a good first season and then I had my injury," said Malacia. "I don't want to talk too much about it, but certain things happened in my rehab.

"Ruben came in when I just got back from my injury. He gave me a couple of games, but I had come back after a year and a half. Imagine not playing for a year and a half and adapting to everything, especially in the best league in the world and playing for such a big club. It takes time.

"As a player you need to understand if you play for a big club like Manchester United, sometimes you don't get the time."

Malacia made eight appearances before joining PSV Eindhoven on loan for the rest of the 2024-25 campaign.

"Even at that time I still wasn't 100%, but it was good for me to get game time and adapting to the game," he said.

"After that period of six months, I came back in summer I thought 'OK, now it's going happen, I'm going to get a fair chance'."

Sadly, for Malacia, his hopes were not realised.

Just before the return for pre-season training, United announced Malacia, Marcus Rashford, Jadon Sancho, Alejandro Garnacho and Antony would train separately from Amorim's squad and would be allowed to leave the club if a suitable offer was made.

It was never clear what Malacia had done wrong as sources say he was not disruptive or a bad influence.

As it turned out, the other four moved on, while Malacia remained in exile at Carrington, training with the under-21s, or even the under-18 and under-17 squads, at his request, to stay in shape.

"I don't know where that came from, I don't know if it was Ruben or higher up or anything, but I never said anything about it, I just kept working and doing my thing even though it was difficult sometimes training in a group of five," he said.

"At some point Marcus, Garnacho and even Antony left. Then I stayed on my own, training with the second team, even with the under-18s and below. It's tough. It's tough mentally.

"I could have said 'OK, I'm not coming into training'. But I thought 'that's not going to help me'. It's a reason for them to say 'this is the reason you are with them or training on your own'. I just kept my head down and did the work.

"I always stayed fit since I came back from my injury, but people didn't know that. They were like 'why is he not playing?'."

Malacia returned to the fold at the end of September 2025.

He was in Amorim's squad for the 25 October encounter with Brighton, and all United's matchday squads from 24 November onwards. He came on for the final two minutes against Newcastle on Boxing Day, the last five in the return at St James' Park on 5 March and made his farewell appearance at Brighton on 24 May.

"I had a good conversation with Michael [Carrick] when he came," said Malacia. "Obviously, I wanted to leave, then some injuries came so I couldn't leave because of the numbers in the squad.

"That was difficult to accept. I was like 'I'm not going to play but I'm not allowed to leave so what's the point of me staying here'. Then he explained to me.

"At the end of the day everybody is there for themselves. I'm there for myself obviously in the first place and then obviously the team but also the manager is there for himself, he needs to save his job or do his job well.

"Still, I don't regret anything. I had a great time in my first season and the people who worked there and the players I met there were amazing, so, nah, I really enjoyed my time."

Malacia is relishing being given the chance to play again.…

items.title: 'We'll get it back' - Carrick responds to criticism
items.content: <article>Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick says "there's a resilience about this football club" as he responds to criticism after a poor run of form.</article>

items.title: Carrick refuses to rule out dropping Fernandes in emotional address
items.content: <article>Michael Carrick speaks for five uninterrupted minutes at media briefing to outline what Manchester United means to him, then refuses to rule out dropping Bruno Fernandes.</article>
items.lbText:
Under-pressure Manchester United boss Michael Carrick delivered a passionate and emotional address lasting five minutes and 30 seconds as he battles to save his job.

And he refused to rule out dropping skipper Bruno Fernandes for Sunday's Premier League meeting with Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

Instead of taking his seat and answering questions as normal in Friday's scheduled pre-match media conference at Carrington, Carrick said he wanted to start himself.

It was a strategy former boss Sir Alex Ferguson used, although the legendary Scot rarely spoke at such length.

After a run of seven games without a win, culminating in Wednesday's shocking 4-1 Champions League defeat by Como, and attacks on the club's hierarchy by defender Lisandro Martinez and then Fernandes' condemnation of his own tactics in Italy, Carrick wanted to reaffirm his view of what United stood for.

"Recently we haven't had a good time, I think that's pretty obvious," he said.

"Wednesday was a bad night, and it hurt me to see us play like that. It was unacceptable.

"My responsibility is to get a team on the pitch that represents this football club, and the supporters, and they can be proud of in the identity we show. We have gone away from that recently. It's important we all recognise that.

"The foundation and values of this football club have been etched for many years. I totally understand and get every single one of them.

"There's a resilience about this football club that runs very deep. I've seen it with my own eyes, I've felt it, I'm know some of the individuals closely who have been a big part of that history.

"Entitlement cannot be at this football club.

"It was based on being humble, having humility, and hard work. We can never lose that, and I won't let us lose that."

Asked about Fernandes and whether he has considered dropping him, a defiant Carrick added: "The most important thing for me is the team, the squad and dynamics in the squad.

"It's about the football club. I'll always do what is best for the football club."

Conte plays down 'unfounded' Man Utd speculation

Should Man Utd boss Carrick drop captain Fernandes?

Have Man Utd become the unmanageable club?

Club sources said on Thursday Fernandes would not have the captaincy taken away or be fined for his post-match observations following the Como defeat.

In a further interview on Wednesday night with Sky Italia, the Portugal international referred to Manchester United's storied history.

"At this club, there's too much focus on what's been done in the past," said Fernandes. "But we're not those people anymore. The club and the players need to understand that.

"Unfortunately for us - especially when it comes to the players - those who join expect to win trophies, win games, and reach the highest level, that's been very difficult at this club in recent years."

Whether Carrick was aware of Fernandes' comments about United's history before he spoke was uncertain.

When asked again if he would take the captaincy away from the 32-year-old midfielder, Carrick repeated: "I will always do what is best for the football club."

He then refused to say whether he had spoken to Fernandes about his conduct, adding: "I don't think this is the time to go into too much detail."

Despite the challenge to his authority, Carrick said the United dressing room was not divided.

"No, it's not," he added. "We just need to get back to doing what we do best."

Carrick also said the club were 'doing everything' to support Fernandes and his family, whose Cheshire home was burgled on Wednesday.

"Thankfully they weren't directly affected even though it is an awful situation."

Carrick named legendary United figures such as Ryan Giggs, Wayne Rooney and Ferguson as examples of the humility, sacrifice and hard work expected of United players.

That was at odds with his post-match criticism on Wednesday, when he said if you don't run forward or back properly, you will not win games.

Asked how he would persuade his current squad to adhere to the values expected and he demanded, Carrick added: "It's clear as day.

"I'm not telling you anything new. I haven't invented that. That's the make-up of any good football team. You have to earn the right to be better than your opponent. That never changes.

"What we look like as a group is my responsibility. That's the privileged position I am in. I'll hold that umbrella for me to get wet and everyone else to stay dry.

"[Wednesday] hurts an awful lot, but that doesn't stop me. That hurt is used as pure motivation and inspiration to want more, expect more and get us going in a different direction."

items.title: Conte plays down 'unfounded' Man Utd speculation
items.content: <article>Antonio Conte says he is not in advanced talks with any club, in response to speculation he has held talks with Manchester United. </article>
items.lbText:
Antonio Conte has said he is not in "advanced negotiations" with any club in response to reports he has held talks with Manchester United.

Italian newspaper La Repubblica , external claimed on Thursday that Conte had held talks with United's board about replacing Michael Carrick following the 4-1 defeat against Como on Wednesday.

The report said the former Chelsea manager had demanded full control of United's transfer policy and stated his intention to appoint his own staff at Old Trafford.

But, while BBC Sport understands Conte is keen on the job, the Italian says he is not in "advanced" talks with any club.

"My name has been linked with numerous clubs, but there are currently no negotiations at an advanced stage," Conte wrote on Instagram.

"I have read reports of financial demands and requests for full control that I have supposedly already made to the clubs mentioned, as well as reservations about what has been described as my "strong personality". These reports are unfounded.

"Should a concrete opportunity arise, that will be the time to hold discussions with the club concerned and jointly consider the terms of a potential agreement, with due regard for both parties' needs and the qualities and approach that define my work as a manager."

Carrick's future at Old Trafford is uncertain after a humiliating defeat to Cesc Fabregas' Como in the Champions League earlier this week.

Although Carrick is set to remain in charge for Sunday's Premier League match against Bournemouth, sources have told BBC Sport that United have begun the process of identifying possible replacements.

Former Newcastle boss Eddie Howe, Conte and ex-Germany manager Julian Nagelsmann are all understood to have their eyes on the job.

Conte is a free agent after leaving Napoli at the end of last season.

He won the Serie A title during his first season in Naples, before a Supercoppa Italiana victory in his final campaign.

items.title: Former Man United chief Murtough joins Birmingham
items.content: <article>Birmingham City appoint ex-Manchester United chief John Murtough as director of football.</article>
items.lbText:
Birmingham City have appointed former Manchester United chief John Murtough as their new director of football.

Murtough, 55, who left United in April 2024 as football director after 11 years at Old Trafford, becomes the replacement for Craig Gardner, who departed St Andrew's in June.

Murtough, who has also worked for Everton, Fulham and Coventry City, was with the Premier League before joining Manchester United in 2013.

His most recent role was in Serie A as director of global development at Atalanta.

Murtough will begin his role at US-owned Birmingham on Monday - following this weekend's Championship game at Cardiff City.

Blues currently sit fourth in the Championship after a run of three straight wins since the international break under head coach Chris Davies.

Birmingham Sports Quarter - what you need to know

In a statement, Birmingham have said Davies "will report into" Murtough, who will report directly into the Blues board.

Murtough will also "collaborate with Hope Powell to ensure that the Blues women's team, enjoy "continued development benefits from the club's wider football strategy".

Blues, twice Women's Super League runners-up in 2011 and 2012, currently sit 13th, one place off the bottom, in the table.

"This is a great football club with brilliant fans and enormous potential" said Murtough. "There is a clear determination from Knighthead to build something special for the long term, both on and off the pitch."

In a board statement, owners Knighthead Capital Management said: "We have been clear from the outset about our ambition for this club and for the city of Birmingham.

"We want Birmingham City competing at the highest level of English football and we are building for sustained success, both on and off the pitch."

Murtough began his career working alongside David Moyes at Everton as a sports scientist, working his way up to become head of performance before leaving in 2012 to become Premier League head of elite performance.

He then joined Man United in 2013, going on to become head of football development, before being promoted to football director in March 2020 a role that gave him "overall leadership and responsibility for operations and strategy across all football functions".

He was at the helm in an era that brought the sacking of Ole Gunnar Solksjaer , the short-term appointments of Michael Carrick and then Ralf Rangnick , before the unveiling of Erik ten Hag . But he had left before ten Hag was sacked in October 2024 .

Jadon Sancho , for £73m, Anthony, the second-most expensive player in the club's history when he signed from Ajax for £81.3m, Rasmus Hojlund for £72m and Mason Mount , for £55m, were all recruited under his watch.

items.title: Should Man Utd boss Carrick drop captain Fernandes?
items.content: <article>Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick must decide whether to leave skipper Bruno Fernandes out of Sunday's crucial Premier League clash with Bournemouth</article>
items.lbText:
Michael Carrick is never short of advice around how he should do his job as head coach of Manchester United.

Few of his players divide opinion quite so much as skipper Bruno Fernandes.

So, it stands to reason there are a variety of views around whether Fernandes should be dropped for Sunday's vital Premier League game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

Former Everton and Rangers striker Duncan Ferguson has no doubts.

"It is a big problem for Michael," he told The Overlap podcast. "Put people in the team you trust. Your captain has thrown you under the bus. If you don't think he is playing for you, get him out. I wouldn't pick him even though he is their best player."

Joe Smith, respected host of Manchester United fan channel Stretford Paddock, is of the same opinion.

"I don't think Fernandes should play on the weekend," he said. "I don't think (Lisandro) Martínez should've played against Leeds, because otherwise they're running the ship here."

United fans heading back on flights from Como to Manchester had a view, although much of it was wrapped up in their general thoughts about the club, most of which were negative.

But only one man's opinion really counts. Carrick is the man who picks the team.

His friend and former team-mate Wayne Rooney has a view on that.

"When Martinez came out, I said this is an absolute nightmare because it will rip the dressing room apart," he said on the United Stand podcast.

"That was the start. We've seen it now with Bruno and you're going to see it with more players because they don't want to take responsibility.

"I was in that situation [as manager at Plymouth and Birmingham City] and if I was in Carrick's position now, I'd come out fighting. There's no more Mr Nice Guy."

Carrick is due to speak in a news conference to preview the Bournemouth game at 1330 BST.

He will be asked whether Bruno Fernandes is going to be dropped.

Many observers were shocked to discover Fernandes was not going to be disciplined for his post-match outburst following the 4-1 Champions League defeat by Como. They were also surprised that he would remain as Manchester United skipper, when team-mate Lisandro Martinez was fined for attacking the club hierarchy eight days earlier after the 2-0 loss to Atletico Madrid.

"It was an assassination," one source who has worked with Fernandes previously, told BBC Sport of Wednesday's comments.

"It was unprofessional. Michael's team are killing him."

The issue is whether Fernandes went too far in attacking Carrick's tactics for the Como game, then saying it was on the coaching team on the sidelines to spot the problem and change it, not the players.

Fernandes is one of the most knowledgeable members of Carrick's squad when it comes to football tactics, and is desperate to succeed. His comments, made on TNT Sports weren't off the cuff, or said in an emotional state after a defeat, as Lisandro Martinez's were.

Yet there is also sympathy for Fernandes from some at Old Trafford given the 32-year-old carried out 10 post-match interviews after the Como debacle, and also because, while hardly offering a defence of Carrick, the words were less inflammatory when they were spoken as they seem in text form.

It is easy to point to Sir Alex Ferguson, the former Manchester United manager who was a strong advocate of managers needing to have control over their players and wonder how he would have reacted to such a situation. Challenges to his authority tended to end with players leaving the club.

However, you only need to listen to Gordon Strachan recounting instances from Ferguson's time in charge at Aberdeen on 'The Good, The Bad and the Football podcast' to accept some of the Scot's more extreme methods would not be acceptable in the current climate.

United's hierarchy are keen to get away from the cycle of sacking managers, having dismissed Ruben Amorim last season and Erik ten Hag in the one before.

However, there is also a basic truth that Carrick desperately needs to end the present run of seven games without a win. If they fail against Bournemouth it would equal the sorry run of Louis van Gaal in 2015-16, which was the worst since a Ferguson-led side had eight draws and a defeat during the 1988-89 season.

So, with Benjamin Sesko, Kobbie Mainoo and Marcus Rashford all ruled out through injury, can Carrick drop Fernandes even if he wanted to?

The Portuguese's link-up with Youri Tielemans has not flourished as imagined.

And the only goal contributions by last season's PFA player of the year have been a hat-trick and assist in the 5-2 win over Ipswich in August and his strike against Azerbaijan champions Sabah FK on 10 September.

But, as Duncan Ferguson said, he is their best player. Carrick has to make the call. He needs to get it right.

items.title: Have Man Utd become the unmanageable club?
items.content: <article>The cycle of doom that has engulfed every Manchester United manager since Sir Alex Ferguson now has Michael Carrick in its unforgiving grip, writes Phil McNulty.</article>
items.lbText:
The cycle of doom that has ultimately engulfed every Manchester United manager since Sir Alex Ferguson now has the hapless Michael Carrick in its unforgiving grip.

Carrick recreated a familiar scene - the same one acted out by predecessor Ole Gunnar Solskjaer after a 4-1 loss at Watford in November 2021 cost him his job - by raising his hands in apology to supporters who had just seen United humiliated by the same scoreline at Como in the Champions League.

Carrick is the seventh full-time manager since Ferguson stepped down in 2013 after winning 38 trophies during 26 years in charge.

Since then there have been days of success under Louis van Gaal, Jose Mourinho and Erik ten Hag, and moments of hope, but the final outcome is always the same - dismissal.

Carrick will need something miraculous to change that storyline, with results poor and revolt within the dressing room as defender Lisandro Martinez took aim at director of football Jason Wilcox after the Champions League defeat at Atletico Madrid, while captain Bruno Fernandes questioned the tactics in Como.

It hints at something rotten in the state of United.

So should it really be crestfallen managers standing in front of those disappointed supporters?

Can it really be United's managers every time? Should not even more scrutiny now be aimed at those who appointed them, then decided the direction of the club?

Have United effectively, through years of decay, decline and appalling decision-making, become the unmanageable club?

There have been those seven full-time managers - David Moyes, Van Gaal, Mourinho, Solskjaer, Ten Hag, Ruben Amorim and Carrick. There have also been spells as interims for others such as Ryan Giggs, Ralf Rangnick, Ruud van Nistelrooy and Darren Fletcher.

United's leaders, from former executive vice-chairman Ed Woodward to the ruling Glazer family and now part-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe, have effectively tried every trick in the book to recreate the Ferguson era.

Moyes, an ill-starred appointment led by Ferguson, found the job too big for him after leaving Everton . Van Gaal and Mourinho were tried and trusted operators with stellar track records of success at Europe's superpowers. Solskjaer was effectively the anti-Mourinho without any sort of managerial track record that suggested he would succeed at United, but appointed after a successful spell in temporary charge.

Ten Hag got the job on the back of leading a superb young Ajax side to the Champions League semi-final. Amorim was regarded as European coaching's hottest young property when he was lured from Sporting in Lisbon.

All ended up sacked. All eventually found the unwieldy beast that is United impossible to tame.

Van Gaal won the FA Cup in 2016. Mourinho won the League Cup and the Europa League in 2017. Ten Hag won the FA Cup in 2024 with a landmark win against Manchester City .

Slim pickings compared to previous glories.

United, however, have not become a bad or dysfunctional club overnight. They have been heading towards this point ever since the succession plan to Ferguson - not easy, admittedly - was botched so badly.

Carlo Ancelotti, Pep Guardiola and Jurgen Klopp all felt able to resist the lure of Old Trafford, leading to what should have been red faces all round in December 2019, when they were all managing within 35 miles of each other in the north-west but none were at United.

Ancelotti was at Everton , Guardiola was at Manchester City . Klopp was at Liverpool . United had Solskjaer, an over-sentimental choice made on the back of a feelgood interim spell. He lasted less than three years.

With every passing day, Carrick looks like Solskjaer Mark II.

Carrick is a former fan favourite who did well in temporary charge, but whose previous managerial career was a sacking at Championship club Middlesbrough. Solskjaer shared that same unwanted distinction, sacked by Cardiff City in September 2014 after only nine months in charge as they struggled in the Championship.

It has all brought United to the point where the question must be asked. Since Ferguson's departure, has it ever been worse than it is now? In recent times, has there ever been less hope than there is now? Has morale ever been lower than it is now?

United will always find a manager should they require one, but their current parlous circumstances mean they are no longer the attraction they once were.

They will not have the pick of the globe's finest. They will need to persuade someone that there is a future at Old Trafford that contains something other than future dismissal, a sobering state of affairs for the self-styled "biggest club in the world".

Given the current state of United's squad, there is no guarantee a manager with a high-class track record would have a quick fix, or any fix at all, without huge investment.

Carrick is front of house and, on current evidence, will pay the price for United's failings. He is a repeat of the Solskjaer mistake, an easy choice made after taking them back into the Champions League, a comfort blanket with supporters that has now been torn away by poor results.

There are significant culprits elsewhere, led by Ratcliffe.

United fans have held regular protests against the Glazers since they took control in 2005, their leveraged purchase loading debt on to the club. They have remained majority owners, despite the level of angered aimed towards them from supporters, unmoved by years of ill feeling.

In turn, Ratcliffe's move into part-ownership alongside the Glazer family has meant fans turned on him for his association and business partnership with the hugely unpopular Americans.

Ratcliffe, like other successful billionaires before him, has found running a football club is a different world to the one he inhabited previously.

He has suggested he leaves big footballing decisions to others, such as Wilcox and chief executive Omar Berrada, but instability and rank bad decisions have come with Ratcliffe as United's leading figure.…

items.title: Fernandes' home burgled while in Italy with Man Utd
items.content: <article>Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes had his home burgled on Wednesday while he was in Italy for his club's Champions League game against Como.</article>
items.lbText:
Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes had his home burgled on Wednesday while he was in Italy for his club's Champions League game against Como.

It is understood Fernandes' family were not in the house in Cheshire when it was broken into and that the intruders were inside for less than five minutes before police arrived.

United are understood to be supporting the 32-year-old following the break-in.

BBC Sport has contacted Cheshire Police about the incident.

He is the latest player to have his family home burgled while playing for his team.

Manchester City player Ruben Dias and former girlfriend Maya Jama also had their Cheshire home burgled in similar circumstances to Fernandes.

Dias was at City's Champions League game against Galatasaray when his home was targeted in January.

Previous victims in the same area include footballers Jack Grealish, Raheem Sterling and Riyad Mahrez.

Portugal midfielder Fernandes has been with Manchester United since joining from Sporting in January 2020.

United were beaten 4-1 by Como and, following the match, Fernandes criticised his manager Michael Carrick's tactics.

However, he will remain as the club's captain and will not be disciplined for his comments.

items.title: Fernandes to stay captain as Rooney calls Man Utd players babies
items.content: <article>Bruno Fernandes will remain as Manchester United captain and will not be disciplined for his post-match criticism of Michael Carrick after the 4-1 Champions League defeat by Como.</article>
items.lbText:
Bruno Fernandes will remain as Manchester United captain and will not be disciplined for his post-match criticism of Michael Carrick after the 4-1 Champions League defeat by Como .

The United skipper criticised Carrick's tactics for the game, then said it was up to the United head coach and his backroom team, not the players, to spot any issues and change them.

It was seen by many externally as a challenge to Carrick's authority, just eight days after United defender Lisandro Martinez criticised director of football Jason Wilcox and the club's summer recruitment.

Inside Old Trafford, there is sympathy for Fernandes for the position he found himself in.

The Portugal midfielder did 10 post-match interviews in Como, despite being replaced by Joshua Zirkzee midway through the second half.

While there is disappointment at some of his comments, it is acknowledged Fernandes' annoyance was understandable given the manner of the loss, which was one of the worst in United's European history.

It remains to be seen whether Fernandes will be picked for Sunday's Premier League encounter with Bournemouth at Old Trafford. Carrick will be asked about the situation when he holds his pre-game news conference at 13:30 BST on Friday.

Fernandes has home burgled while in Italy with Man Utd

Carrick carrying on but senior Man Utd figures concerned by performances

Former Manchester United striker Wayne Rooney said he was in "shock" and "disbelief" at the performance against Como and he is as "worried as I've been for a long time" at the situation at Old Trafford.

And, while he understands the questioning of Carrick, a close personal friend of the former England and United skipper, Rooney also called the players "selfish" and said "they're like babies" in the wake of the controversial comments from both Martinez and Fernandes.

"When Martinez came out, I said this is an absolute nightmare because it will rip the dressing room apart," Rooney told the United Stand podcast. "That was the start. We've seen it now with Bruno and you're going to see it with more players because they don't want to take responsibility.

"You can say whether Bruno was right or wrong in what he said but you have to take responsibility on the pitch. You have to take responsibility as a group of players.

"These players, they're selfish. They don't care about their team-mates, don't care about the manager, the staff or the fans, they care about themselves. If they're not getting what's right for them, they're like babies and just throw their toys out of the pram and go and deflect the blame on to anyone else but themselves."

Fernandes' form has dipped markedly from last season, when he was named PFA and FWA Player of the Year and broke the Premier League record for assists in a single season.

"He [Fernandes] is putting pressure on someone else because he doesn't want to face it," added Rooney.

"If he looks at himself in the mirror, if Martinez and all of them looked at themselves in the mirror, they'll find what's looking back at them is them, and that's not good enough. They need to show more."

Rooney has also called on the Manchester United board to provide clarity on the future of Carrick, who he believes needs to "come out fighting".

Carrick will be in charge for Sunday's visit of Bournemouth despite intense speculation he is on the brink of dismissal following United's worst run of form since 2015-16.

"I was in that situation [at Plymouth and Birmingham City] and I can only say now, looking back and reflecting, if I was in Michael Carrick's position now, I'd come out fighting," said Rooney.

"There's no more Mr Nice Guy. There are certain things you've got to do to protect them players, but you have to come out fighting for yourself because those players will drag you down and it's going to be you who's going to lose your job over it."

items.title: Carrick carrying on but senior Man Utd figures concerned by performances
items.content: <article>While head coach Michael Carrick is expected to be in charge for Sunday's match against Bournemouth, Manchester United begin the process of identifying possible replacements.</article>
items.lbText:
While head coach Michael Carrick is expected to be in charge for Sunday's match against Bournemouth, Manchester United have already begun the process of identifying possible replacements.

Eddie Howe, Antonio Conte and Julian Naglesmann are understood to have their eyes on the Old Trafford job.

Sources say Carrick is carrying on as normal and has not been made aware of any imminent change following Wednesday's humiliating 4-1 defeat by Italian side Como.

That defeat was followed by captain Bruno Fernandes questioning Carrick's tactics in the Champions League loss.

The players have been given Thursday off, while United are still to confirm arrangements for Friday's planned news conference to preview the Bournemouth match.

Some senior figures at United are of the view that chopping and changing mangers so regularly in recent years has failed to arrest United's decline, and that Carrick has been let down by players who are under-performing.

That does not necessarily mean that Carrick is safe, of course.

There remains major uncertainty over his future. But there is also an appreciation in some quarters of the progress that he and his squad made last season, and a view that he should be given more time to turn things around.

For weeks, managers - in and out of work - have grown aware that the United job may become available.

Howe, for example, is available and would be considered. Sources have indicated that the former Newcastle boss is open to returning to management with Manchester United after leaving St James' Park in the close season.

Former Chelsea boss Conte and ex-Germany manager Naglesmann, who are also out of work, are also interested.

Aston Villa head coach Unai Emery and Brighton boss Fabian Hurzeler's stock is high with those in the corridors of power at United - but extracting them away from their respective clubs would be difficult.

'Not what a captain should be' - the debate around Fernandes' outburst

Man Utd humbling by Como leaves Carrick job in danger

For the third year in a row, United have publicly and financially backed a manager in the summer, but positive results have not followed.

Ruben Amorim staggered on to January, but the shock League Cup defeat at League Two side Grimsby last August and the awful performance at Brentford less than a month later stripped away his safety net and gave United's hierarchy nowhere to go when he attacked their influence.

United looked extensively at other candidates, including Thomas Tuchel and Roberto de Zerbi, in the summer of 2024 before deciding to stick with Erik ten Hag. The Dutchman was dismissed in the October.

There were dissenting voices when he was appointed on a permanent basis in May, but the majority of supporters felt 12 wins from 17 in interim charge and a place in the Champions League after a two-year absence meant the 45-year-old former United midfielder deserved a crack at the job.

There are numerous reasons behind the club's poor form this season and blame can be apportioned across a variety of departments and to the very top of the club.

However, the brutal truth is two wins from 11 games, and none in seven, their worst run since 2015-16 when eight matches without a win took Louis van Gaal to the brink of dismissal, is simply not good enough. And as head coach, Carrick bears significant responsibility for that.

Accusations of a lack of passion, desire and intensity have dogged United all season, having won just two of their matches in all competitions.

The team has also been hampered by injuries and players failing to reach the level anticipated.

While they have struggled in attack, they have also only kept a single clean sheet all season as form, results and confidence have all dipped.

Mixed into that negativity has come explosive post-match comments from experienced defender Lisandro Martinez, attacking the recruitment, and Fernandes, attacking Carrick and his tactics.

In between was the interview in the Athletic with Ten Hag when he spoke of 'broken promises' and a 'toxic culture'. It all smacks of a club lacking control, discipline and a clear forward-looking strategy.

There is certainly a view from senior figures around the club that while overall recruitment can be questioned – specifically the strategy of strengthening midfield in the most recent transfer window, at the expense of bringing in striking support for Benjamin Sesko or competition at left-back for Luke Shaw, part of a long list of absentees in Como – the players have to take a significant amount of responsibility for the current situation.

Whether that helps Carrick is another matter.

The proximity of United's next Premier League game doesn't make immediate change straightforward even if that was the thinking.

Following Amorim's dismissal in January, former United midfielder Darren Fletcher took over as interim manager for two games. Fletcher subsequently returned to his role as Under-18 coach, but two of the coaches who helped him, Jonny Evans and Travis Binnion, stayed with the senior set-up as part of Carrick's team.

United have a clear midweek coming up following their EFL Cup defeat by Brighton, who came back from two down to win at Old Trafford last month. That, in theory, would allow time to take stock without the immediate pressure a match can bring.

Bournemouth secured their first Premier League win under new boss Marco Rose last week. They drew 4-4 in a memorable encounter at Old Trafford last season, prior to that, they won 3-0 on both of their previous two visits.

It remains to be seen if Carrick will be in charge, and if so, how long after that.

It seems the only certainty around Manchester United just now, is the sense of uncertainty – again.

items.title: Breaking down Man Utd's tactics after Fernandes' criticism
items.content: <article>Was Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes correct in his analysis of his side's tactics in their 4-1 thrashing by Italian side Como?</article>
items.lbText:
Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes appeared to question their tactical approach after Wednesday's 4-1 Champions League defeat by Como.

"We started off on the wrong foot," the Portuguese said. "They scored very early, [we had] not much pressure on the ball.

"It's a decision from the staff to not press man-to-man and sometimes leave some space behind, to try and get the ball in the first moment [by] waiting for them, [giving] them the ball.

"Sometimes when you give too much of the ball to these teams, they get confidence. They have so many bodies behind the ball, they make you run a lot, people get frustrated."

His quotes are tactically dense so warrant breaking down, but what did Fernandes mean, and does he have a point?

Since Michael Carrick became United manager in January, they have largely defended in a zonal 4-2-4 or 4-4-2 shape that springs into a press in moments.

When Fernandes said United "leave some space behind, to try and get the ball in the first moment" he was referring to them not immediately pressing across the pitch in a man-to-man fashion.

Holding their 4-2-4 shape a little bit deeper, United allow opposition defenders time and space on the ball, looking to set traps before pouncing.

The overarching idea is with four players narrow and high, United's attackers are well positioned to score from turnovers should they win the ball back.

At times during Carrick's stint as caretaker head coach last season, it worked well - as we saw when Bryan Mbeumo scored in United's 3-2 win at Arsenal in January two weeks after Carrick took over

But the same approach has been less effective this season.

On the same night defender Lisandro Martinez questioned United's recruitment - after their 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid - he also spoke about the ever-changing tactical landscape.

"You can't stay with what you did last season." he said. "Teams know you, how you play, know every detail, and if you don't change, next season is a big problem."

Last season, the introduction of the 4-2-4 shape as a defensive tactic caught a number of teams off guard, making it more effective.

Pep Guardiola and Pep Lijnders used the same shape at Manchester City - a tweak that underpinned their Carabao Cup final win over an ill-prepared Arsenal .

Having replaced Guardiola, Enzo Maresca redeployed it for the Community Shield in August, but this time Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta had the solutions and the Gunners won.

Within a few games, Maresca had abandoned the 4-24 and moved to a more man-to-man style of defending.

Perhaps that is the sort of change Fernandes is hoping for - recognising the reduced effectiveness of United's defensive approach, with signs of weakness visible as early as pre-season.

AC Milan - now managed by former United boss Ruben Amorim - repeatedly found joy playing around the 4-2-4, with a back five that outnumbered the Red Devils' front four.

United's two central attackers would look to block passes into Milan's midfield two before pressing the central defenders.

The wide position of one of the central defenders would force a United winger to step out, and Milan's wing-back - dropping deep and wide - gave them an easy way out.

United's full-back would then have to cover a large distance to close down the wing-back but by the time pressure was applied, the ball was gone.

The same problems were seen in United's defeat by Atletico Madrid.

Atletico took the risk of employing the same tactic with a back four rather than a back five, which left them an extra attacker high up the pitch.

As United's front two looked to stop passes into the central midfielders, the wide position of the centre-backs drew out United's wingers.

That, in turn, meant left-back Alejandro Grimaldo found himself in space out wide.

This required Diogo Dalot, or if he was pinned back by winger Alex Baena, Youri Tielemans to cover large distances in an attempt to apply some pressure to Grimaldo.

So while Fernandes may have been referring to himself when he said "they make you run a lot, people get frustrated", it could easily have applied to these team-mates.

When Fernandes' quotes were put to Carrick after the game, he pushed back.

"We actually half-pressed, man-to-man in the second half and then ended up conceding a goal from that," he said.

"It's a little bit on whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, but if you don't run and you don't run forward and you don't run back, you aren't going to win."

While the less aggressive 4-2-4 has its weaknesses, it often leaves an extra player in the backline, giving United a numerical advantage in defence.

It also aims to funnel attacks down the flanks, where they are - in theory - less dangerous than chances conceded through the middle.

United's backline have also - under both Carrick and Amorim - struggled to track and duel with their opponents in one-against-one situations when they have committed to a full press.

When using a man-to-man press, losing an individual battle, or lacking the intensity to arrive at your opposing player quickly, makes the system fall apart as we saw for Como's second goal.

In the Premier League, United have also had spells during which they have attempted to press in a more man-to-man fashion, but these have also been imperfectly executed.

In fact, against Spurs , it was Fernandes who misread moments and positioned himself incorrectly.

Despite Amorim's flaws, one of his strengths was in improving United's physical base and intensity. There is a question as to whether Carrick's United, with one game a week last season, were beneficiaries of that.

This season they look unable to sustain the intensity to execute a man-to-man press with the effectiveness of, say, Fabian Hurzeler's Brighton - a physically fit squad aligned on how and when to press.

For United, more concerningly, there appears to be a disconnect - at least in how Fernandes sees the game and the messaging from the coaching staff.…

items.title: 'Not what a captain should be' - the debate around Fernandes' outburst
items.content: <article>Bruno Fernandes' comments after Manchester United's humbling by Como have got fans and pundits talking - but what now for the captain?</article>
items.lbText:
Bruno Fernandes' comments after Manchester United's humbling by Como have got fans and pundits talking - but what now for the captain?

United's 4-1 Champions League defeat in Italy was the result of a wretched performance and Fernandes questioned boss Michael Carrick's tactics.

"It's a decision from the staff to not press man-to-man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, but sometimes when you give too much the ball to these teams they get confidence," said the Portugal attacking midfielder on TNT Sports.

Asked if Carrick got his tactics wrong, the 32-year-old continued: "That's on the manager and staff to see it, not me."

Fernandes rounds on Carrick after Man Utd humiliation

Man Utd humbling by Como leaves Carrick job in danger

Not according to former Liverpool vice-captain Jamie Carragher, working as a summariser, on CBS Sports.

"He's reacted like that because he's been embarrassed by the manager [who] brought him off," said the ex-England defender.

"And when he talks about pressing, whether it's man-to-man or zonal, for years, Bruno Fernandes has meant Manchester United can't press because he does things for the crowd.

"He runs all over the place like a kid in the schoolyard for the supporters. They all think he's working hard. He's not. He's killing the rest of the team doing it."

He added: "Watching him throw his arms up every week in a game is an absolute disgrace [and] calling the manager out considering how he's performed this season on the pitch.

"[It's an] awful attitude and not what a Manchester United captain should be."

Fernandes' comments come a week after defender Lisandro Martinez made similar headlines following United's previous Champions League defeat by Atletico Madrid.

The Argentine said he expected more investment in the squad and "more from our technical director [Jason Wilcox]". He later apologised.

And while Martinez's outburst sparked debate, Fernandes' comments could have even larger repercussions.

Carrick, who was under huge pressure already following a terrible start to the season, said in reply: "There's a little bit of whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, if you don't run, and you don't run forward, and you don't run back, you aren't going to win."

United have not won in their past seven games since beating Champions League minnows Sabah. They have just one win in their seven Premier League games this season.

Not many people have defended Fernandes' public questioning of the tactics.

But some do understand his frustrations.

Former Leicester and Celtic keeper Kasper Schmeichel, whose dad Peter won the Champions League, five Premier League titles and three FA Cups as a United player, said on BBC Radio 5 Live: "Given last week and what's happened, he probably should not be saying these things because it's only going to add to the problems.

"With experience you learn that you need to keep these things in-house. It's a problem, with everything that happened during the week.

"Michael Carrick didn't need this, the club didn't need this. It's exposing all of the issues that are at Manchester United.

"It's very plain to see that there are loads of issues but you need to be fixing them, you need to be having meetings within the club, which I'm sure that they are, but it's obviously not resolved. It's just translating on to the pitch."

The issue that most pundits have is not that Fernandes has these opinions - but that he has let the world know them.

Former Liverpool defender Stephen Warnock, speaking on BBC Match of the Day, said: "I think there will be ex-players now from Manchester United saying, 'why are you letting this get out, this should be a collective in the changing room where we come together'.

"Whether you like the manager or not, you've got to come together and say 'OK how do we correct this?'

"Senior players go to the manager and say 'listen we didn't agree with the tactics, we didn't think we got it right, how do we go about this, how do we move forward', because you start airing it in public and it doesn't end well for anyone."

Former Chelsea midfielder Joe Cole on TNT Sports called it "sacrilege".

"I've played for managers where I don't agree with the tactics but you might say that to your mate or to your wife. You don't come out as captain of the club and question the manager," he said.

Andy Mitten, editor of United We Stand, told BBC 5 Live Breakfast that Fernandes has "thrown his coach under the bus".

"And Manchester United fans are divided as to whether he should or should not do that. Last week, Martinez was also critical. A lot of Manchester United fans agreed with him.

"Again, there's mitigation, he wants a new contract. That's because he's not been playing enough, because he's been injured. And injuries are a real problem for Manchester United. There's no recognised centre-forward. So it is a really difficult time for United."

Former United midfielder Carrick, who took over in January initially as caretaker manager, seemed to blank his players at full-time before heading over to the United fans.

"I don't blame him for ignoring the players," said Mitten.

"He went to the fans and he held his hands up and he said, 'I'm sorry'.

"You can tell he's hurting. He's a Manchester United fan himself. He was a season ticket holder only a year ago before he took the job. I think he's trying his best, but it's just not working at the moment. Manchester United are really, really struggling."

Fernandes has been Manchester United's one consistent outstanding player since a £47m move from Sporting in January 2020, when Ole Gunnar Solskjaer was the manager.

He has scored 111 goals and made 106 assists in 338 games for the club in all competitions.

Former manager Erik ten Hag made him the skipper in the summer of 2023 after taking the armband off Harry Maguire, whose place in the team was far from certain.…

items.title: Paz, Fabregas and Como teach Man Utd a lesson
items.content: <article>Serie A success story Como have gone from Serie D to the Champions League - now they have taught Manchester United a lesson in Europe.</article>
items.lbText:
When Manchester United savoured the last of their three Champions League triumphs in 2008, Como were a Serie D club, playing in one of nine semi-professional regional leagues.

On Wednesday, at a rainy but picturesque Giuseppe Sinigaglia Stadium on the banks of the iconic Lake Como, the Serie A outfit showed how far they have come.

In fact, on the evidence of their 4-1 thrashing of the English side - and with progressive coach Cesc Fabregas in the dugout - you could argue the European newcomers have leapfrogged the Old Trafford outfit and then some.

Time and again, Fabregas' side sliced through United - who are now winless in their past seven games in all competitions for the first time since 2015.

At the heart of Fabregas' team is the brilliant Nico Paz, signed from Real Madrid in 2024, who scored twice and set up another.

Since the start of September, the 22-year-old Tenerife-born Argentina international has been directly involved in more goals in all competitions than any other Serie A player.

"It was a historic night because we played against one of the best teams ever, to do this at home is incredible, we are very happy for our performance," said Paz.

Wednesday's superb showing took him to nine goal involvements in eight appearances - four goals and five assists - he is also the youngest Argentine player to be involved in three goals in one Champions League game since Lionel Messi against Bayern Munich in April 2009.

"He's been absolutely brilliant in everything that he has done," said Glenn Hoddle on TNT. "A lot of his play has been creative and risky, but he's pulled it off."

For Como, this is the most high-profile victory since their project began.

"It's Manchester United. We are only just getting our heads around the fact we are playing Inter, Milan and Juventus," said one member of staff.

"This is without doubt the biggest night in the club's history."

According to chief executive Mirwan Surwaso, it was Como's status as an amateur club - they returned to Serie D in 2017 after being unable to convince the authorities of their financial wellbeing - which first attracted the London-based media company Sent Entertainment, owned by Indonesian billionaires Robert Budi Hartono and Michael Bambang Hartono.

When they concluded a deal in 2019, the Hartono brothers were planning a TV project, with the idea of screening matches involving young Indonesian players back home. A visit from Manchester United was not part of the plan.

There cannot be many Champions League stadiums you can walk around and in addition to seeing an iconic tourist attraction. Lake Como is 29 miles long and 2.5 miles wide in some parts - you also come across a yacht club and an 'Aero Club' for the sea-planes that take off at regular intervals.

The clubs themselves have been there for a long time. But Como also use their natural surroundings to offer one hour Lake Como tours, followed by 'pre-match Lakeside hospitality'.

In town - Como's population is just over 83,000, which means 90% of them could fit in the San Siro Stadium - there is a plush new club shop, selling all kinds of branded merchandise. There was no need for that in Serie D.

"Somehow the team got promoted, we had to go professional, and the plan had to be scrapped," Surwaso told Piers Morgan's Football Uncensored Podcast this month.

The alternative plan is still being amended substantially.

Initially it was expected this season would be a selling year, when some of the developing talents Como thought they could cash in on would be sold.

Instead, manager Cesc Fabregas steered his squad to fourth place in 2025-26, capitalising on AC Milan's shock defeat at Cagliari.

It meant in the space of five seasons from Fabregas' arrival as a player, Como had gone from Serie B to the Champions League. Earlier this week, Lionel Messi's son Ciro gave Como his seal of approval by being pictured with his dad wearing a replica Como kit. Tangible evidence of a meteoric rise.

"Compared to when I finished my career here, it is completely different," said Fabregas. "It is not even night and day. It is another world.

"Playing Manchester United is a historic day once again for the club, the city of Como and fanbase.

"When I retired as a player, I coached to get experience. I explained what I thought of the club and my vision and put the plan to work. We are a family here. Even when we lose, fans come and celebrate. We need to be humble and remember who we were because the story of Como will be beautiful, and we will remember it forever."

The captivating nature of the Como story does bring with it some questions.

In the short term, some wonder how they can possibly comply with Uefa's financial rules, which European football's governing body does not intend to amend despite Como's rise from Serie B.

Surwaso told Morgan: "The scrutiny is on us but we always have our books in order, so we are not too worried."

The other point is that three quarters of the 12,300-capacity Stadio Giuseppe Sinigaglia is uncovered and was exposed to heavy rain during the fixture.

Growing both sides of the club is essential if Como are to maximise their potential.

For Fabregas, whose responsibility is clearly on the playing side, there is a balance to be struck between celebrating the spectacular journey Como have been on, and ensuring his players are not resting on their laurels.

"We were at minus 10 when we started, but we don't want to spend time thinking about what has passed," said the former Arsenal, Barcelona and Chelsea star.

"If you want to do that, retire and go write a book about what Como did. We must look at what is in front of us."

While Como now attract thousands to their games, those who followed the club when crowds were in the hundreds remain.

"I had an uncle who supported Como," said Marco Melillo, an out-of-town fan.

"He showed me the sticker collection, I saw the blue shirt and the blue colours and totally went crazy about it.…

items.title: Fernandes rounds on Carrick after Man Utd humiliation
items.content: <article>Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes blames head coach Michael Carrick for the tactics that led to an embarrassing 4-1 defeat by Como in the Champions League.</article>
items.lbText:
Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes turned on head coach Michael Carrick following one of the most humiliating nights in the club's European history.

A 4-1 Champions League hammering at Como led to Carrick fielding questions about his future.

He apologised to the 700 travelling fans, having ignored his beaten players after the final whistle to march across the pitch and repeatedly hold his hands up - in a manner similar to Ole Gunnar Solskjaer following a 4-1 defeat at Watford in November 2021 which led to his dismissal as United boss 24 hours later.

However, Fernandes - widely accepted as a football obsessive who watches games regularly and understands the tactical side as well as any player in the United squad - inflicted more damage when he spoke to TNT Sports afterwards.

"It's a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, but sometimes when you give too much the ball to these teams they get confidence," he said.

Asked directly whether Carrick got his tactics wrong, Fernandes added: "That's on the manager and staff to see it, not me. Sometimes you have to be more brave under pressure, take the risk of pressing high and making them uncomfortable."

Told of Fernandes' comments in his post-match press conference, Carrick offered a curt response: "There's a little bit of whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, if you don't run, and you don't run forward, and you don't run back, you aren't going to win."

Carrick also refused to answer questions about his own future.

Instead, he described his own feelings about United's performance and focused on taking responsibility.

"I have to apologise to the supporters," said the former player. "I care about this football club as much as anyone, if not more, with the position that I'm in and what I value this football club. For us to play in that way is not acceptable.

"I always go over to the fans anyway, regardless, so it wasn't a particularly different kind of reason why I went over.

"It's the appreciation and acknowledgement of what they've gone through and have done over a period of a few weeks now. As I said, I was one of them.

"I'm feeling the same as them. We've got a lot of values in this football club; what we represent and how we want to go about it. We might win, we might lose, but the way we went about it tonight wasn't acceptable. I just wanted to let the fans know that I feel for them.

"Listen. I've not given my own position any thought - this is for the supporters - I was one of them watching that and I wasn't happy all."

Man Utd embarrassment in Como leaves Carrick job in danger

After winning 12 of his 17 games in charge last season to guide United back into the Champions League after a two-year absence, Carrick was given a two-year contract.

However, as happened with Solskjaer five years ago, the new campaign has unravelled spectacularly and they are 13th in the Premier League, three points clear of bottom club Sunderland.

Although they recovered from their shock opening-day defeat to newly promoted Hull by coming from behind to beat Ipswich the following week, United have not won in the Premier League since. Their only other success in 11 games in all competitions came against Azerbaijan champions Sabah FK in the Champions League.

Their latest loss meant they have now gone seven games without a win, their worst run since they went eight without a victory under Louis van Gaal between 25 November and 28 December 2015.

Only Joshua Zirkzee's injury-time consolation prevented United suffering their joint second-worst European defeat of all time.

The embarrassment was heightened by the knowledge that when they were last crowned European champions in 2008, Como were playing semi-professional football in front of a couple of hundred spectators in Serie D.

It is a basic reality that if Como's star man Nico Paz, who opened the scoring after 118 seconds, created the second and added a third goal, said he wanted to leave Como, virtually every big club in Europe would want to sign him and United's chances would be virtually non-existent.

They entertain 15th-placed Bournemouth in the Premier League on Sunday knowing that prior to last season's amazing 4-4 draw, the Cherries recorded 3-0 wins on their previous two visits to Old Trafford.

United flew straight back to Manchester after the game.

It remains to be seen whether the position around Carrick changes before the Bournemouth game. However, United supporters sang against the Glazer family and Sir Jim Ratcliffe as the shambolic evening unravelled.

Both Carrick and sporting director Jason Wilcox have been absolved of partial blame for the club's plight by some; Carrick because he was let down badly in the summer transfer window, when the club signed three midfielders, but failed to bring in competition for Luke Shaw at left-back and Benjamin Sesko in attack. Wilcox too, because he had to work to a budget set by those above him, including chief executive Omar Berrada.

"There was a lot going through my mind watching that," admitted Carrick, who won five Premier League titles and the Champions League during his United playing career. "It was tough to watch.

"It wasn't just the goals, if I'm totally honest. It was was the manner and way we played at times.

"I'm giving my absolute best all the time, I care about it. My whole life is wrapped around it. It might go well, it might not go so well, but I I genuinely give everything that I possibly can."
